strategy_title: Inlining Mask Intermediates Does Not Reduce Instruction Count
strategy_description: Inlining intermediate boolean mask variables directly into tl.load mask arguments (e.g., replacing `tmp10_masked = tmp10 & xmask; tl.load(..., mask=tmp10_masked)` with `tl.load(..., mask=tmp10 & xmask)`) produced no change in executed instruction count (2005080 both before and after) and actually slightly increased elapsed cycles (11204 → 11416) and warp cycles per issued instruction (15.46 → 15.80). The measured speedup of ~1.10x appears to come from the simultaneously added XBLOCK=256 autotune config rather than the mask inlining itself. Inlining mask temporaries is a cosmetic refactor that does not affect compiled PTX or SASS instruction count in Triton.
slow_pseudocode:
tmp10_masked = tmp10 & xmask
tmp11 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + offset, mask=tmp10_masked, other=float('-inf'))
tmp16_masked = tmp16 & xmask
tmp17 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + offset2, mask=tmp16_masked, other=float('-inf'))
# ... repeated for all 9 loads
fast_pseudocode:
tmp11 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + offset, mask=tmp10 & xmask, other=float('-inf'))
tmp17 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + offset2, mask=tmp16 & xmask, other=float('-inf'))
# ... repeated for all 9 loads (no intermediate variable)
applicable_when: Never: inlining boolean mask temporaries into tl.load mask arguments is a purely cosmetic change that does not affect compiled instruction count or memory access patterns in Triton.
do_not_apply_when: Always: this change has no measurable effect on performance. Do not spend optimization budget on mask variable inlining when instruction count and memory access patterns are unchanged.
framework_notes: In Triton, the JIT compiler treats `tmp = a & b; tl.load(..., mask=tmp)` and `tl.load(..., mask=a & b)` identically at the PTX/SASS level. The executed instruction count was identical (2005080) before and after this change, confirming no compiler-level difference. The observed 1.10x speedup is attributable to the addition of a new XBLOCK=256 autotune config in the same diff, not to mask inlining.

strategy_title: evict_last Cache Hint Reduces L1TEX Stall in Pooling Kernels
strategy_description: Adding eviction_policy='evict_last' to all tl.load calls in a 3x3 max_pool2d kernel achieved a modest 1.09x speedup despite the L1/TEX hit rate barely moving (1.41% → 1.5%) and No-Eligible stalls actually worsening (35.6% → 54.9%). The speedup appears to be a confound: the autotune simultaneously added num_warps=1 and num_warps=16 configs, causing autotune to select a 32-thread block (num_warps=1) instead of the prior 64-thread block, which reduced total executed instructions from 2.0M to 1.49M and registers per thread jumped from 32 to 50. The evict_last hint itself did not measurably improve L1 hit rate or reduce L1TEX stall cycles — the CPIStall stall fraction actually increased (50.6% → 59.5%) — suggesting the cache hint had negligible effect on this workload's access pattern.
slow_pseudocode:
# 9 masked loads with default eviction policy
tmp11 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + ((-7920) + x6), mask=tmp10 & xmask, other=float('-inf'))
tmp17 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + ((-7392) + x6), mask=tmp16 & xmask, other=float('-inf'))
# ... 7 more loads ...
tl.store(out_ptr0 + x6, result, mask=xmask)
fast_pseudocode:
# 9 masked loads with evict_last hint (marginal effect on L1 hit rate)
tmp11 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + ((-7920) + x6), mask=tmp10 & xmask, other=float('-inf'), eviction_policy='evict_last')
tmp17 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + ((-7392) + x6), mask=tmp16 & xmask, other=float('-inf'), eviction_policy='evict_last')
# ... 7 more loads ...
tl.store(out_ptr0 + x6, result, mask=xmask)
# NOTE: actual speedup driven by autotune selecting num_warps=1 (32-thread block), not the cache hint
applicable_when: Kernel has near-zero L1/TEX hit rate (<5%), high L2 hit rate (>70%), and CPIStall rule flags L1TEX scoreboard dependency as >50% of stall cycles. The input tensor has spatial locality that could be exploited by neighboring blocks sharing pooling window rows.
do_not_apply_when: The working set per SM wave is much larger than L1 cache capacity (e.g., >192KB on A100/H200), making cross-block L1 reuse impossible regardless of eviction policy. In such cases, evict_last will not improve L1 hit rate and the CPIStall stall fraction may worsen as the hint competes with other data for limited L1 capacity. Also avoid conflating this change with simultaneous autotune config additions — isolate the cache hint change to measure its true effect.
framework_notes: In Triton, eviction_policy='evict_last' maps to the CUDA .ca (cache-all) load modifier on Ampere/Hopper, instructing the GPU to retain the cache line in L1 with high priority. The default Triton policy uses .cg (cache-global, L2 only) or .cs (streaming). However, if the input working set exceeds L1 capacity, this hint provides no benefit. In this experiment, the confounding autotune config change (adding num_warps=1) was the dominant factor — the cache hint alone should be tested in isolation before attributing speedup to it.

strategy_title: Eviction Policy Hints Reduce L1TEX Stalls in Pooling Kernels
strategy_description: Adding eviction_policy='evict_last' to all input loads and eviction_policy='evict_first' to output stores in a 3x3 max-pool kernel reduced L1TEX scoreboard stalls (CPIStall from 50.6% to 32.4% of CPI) and improved scheduler eligibility (Eligible Warps Per Scheduler: 2.58→4.31, No Eligible: 35.6%→24.3%), yielding a modest 8.8% speedup. However, the L1/TEX hit rate barely moved (1.41%→1.51%), indicating the eviction hints did not meaningfully increase cache reuse — the improvement came primarily from reduced stall cycles per instruction (15.46→13.5 cycles/warp) rather than cache hit rate gains. The elapsed cycles actually increased slightly (11204→11525), suggesting the speedup measured at the end-to-end level may reflect reduced scheduling overhead rather than true memory access improvement.
slow_pseudocode:
# 9 masked loads with no eviction policy hints
tmp11 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + ((-7920) + x6), mask=tmp10 & xmask, other=float('-inf'))
tmp17 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + ((-7392) + x6), mask=tmp16 & xmask, other=float('-inf'))
# ... 7 more loads ...
tl.store(out_ptr0 + (x6), tmp51, mask=xmask)
fast_pseudocode:
# 9 masked loads with evict_last; store with evict_first
tmp11 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + ((-7920) + x6), mask=tmp10 & xmask, other=float('-inf'), eviction_policy='evict_last')
tmp17 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + ((-7392) + x6), mask=tmp16 & xmask, other=float('-inf'), eviction_policy='evict_last')
# ... 7 more loads with eviction_policy='evict_last' ...
tl.store(out_ptr0 + (x6), tmp51, mask=xmask, eviction_policy='evict_first')
applicable_when: Kernel has high L1TEX CPIStall (>40% of CPI), very low L1/TEX hit rate (<5%), and performs multiple loads from spatially overlapping neighborhoods (e.g., pooling, convolution, stencil). The stall type is L1TEX scoreboard dependency. Eligible Warps Per Scheduler is low (<3.0) indicating insufficient warp-level latency hiding.
do_not_apply_when: L1/TEX hit rate is already moderate (>10%) or the kernel is purely streaming with no spatial reuse opportunity. Also avoid if instruction count is already high — the after profile shows 25% more executed instructions (2.0M→2.5M), suggesting the eviction policy hints may increase PTX instruction count in some compiler paths. Do not expect large speedups (>20%) from this change alone when block size is small (64 threads / 2 warps), as inter-warp reuse is limited.
framework_notes: In Triton, eviction_policy='evict_last' maps to the .lu PTX cache operator on H100/H200, instructing L1 to retain the cache line longer. eviction_policy='evict_first' maps to .cs (cache streaming), marking the line for early eviction. These are advisory hints; the compiler may not always honor them. The speedup here (8.8%) is modest and the L1 hit rate improvement was negligible (1.41%→1.51%), suggesting the benefit came from scheduler-level effects rather than true cache reuse. The instruction count increase (25%) is an unexpected side effect worth monitoring.

strategy_title: Add evict_last Cache Hint to Stencil/Pooling Loads
strategy_description: Adding eviction_policy='evict_last' to all tl.load calls in a 3x3 max-pool kernel reduced Warp Cycles Per Issued Instruction from 15.46 to 13.28 and improved scheduler eligibility (Eligible Warps Per Scheduler: 2.58 → 3.99, No Eligible: 35.6% → 27.3%), yielding a 7.6% speedup. The dominant stall type shifted from L1TEX dependency stalls (50.6% of stall cycles before) to 'not selected' stalls (31.5% after), indicating the eviction hint successfully reduced L1TEX latency stalls by keeping input lines resident longer in L1. Notably, the L1/TEX hit rate barely changed (1.41% → 1.48%), suggesting the benefit came from reduced eviction pressure and faster L1 servicing rather than a measurable hit-rate increase — the hint likely reduced cache line thrashing under the overlapping 9-point stencil access pattern.
slow_pseudocode:
# 9 masked loads for 3x3 max-pool, no eviction hint
tmp11 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + ((-7920) + x6), mask=pred0 & xmask, other=float('-inf'))
tmp17 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + ((-7392) + x6), mask=pred1 & xmask, other=float('-inf'))
tmp24 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + ((-6864) + x6), mask=pred2 & xmask, other=float('-inf'))
tmp31 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + ((-528)  + x6), mask=pred3 & xmask, other=float('-inf'))
tmp34 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + (x6),           mask=pred4 & xmask, other=float('-inf'))
tmp37 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + (528   + x6),   mask=pred5 & xmask, other=float('-inf'))
tmp44 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + (6864  + x6),   mask=pred6 & xmask, other=float('-inf'))
tmp47 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + (7392  + x6),   mask=pred7 & xmask, other=float('-inf'))
tmp50 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + (7920  + x6),   mask=pred8 & xmask, other=float('-inf'))
fast_pseudocode:
# Same 9 masked loads with eviction_policy='evict_last'
tmp11 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + ((-7920) + x6), mask=pred0 & xmask, other=float('-inf'), eviction_policy='evict_last')
tmp17 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + ((-7392) + x6), mask=pred1 & xmask, other=float('-inf'), eviction_policy='evict_last')
tmp24 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + ((-6864) + x6), mask=pred2 & xmask, other=float('-inf'), eviction_policy='evict_last')
tmp31 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + ((-528)  + x6), mask=pred3 & xmask, other=float('-inf'), eviction_policy='evict_last')
tmp34 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + (x6),           mask=pred4 & xmask, other=float('-inf'), eviction_policy='evict_last')
tmp37 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + (528   + x6),   mask=pred5 & xmask, other=float('-inf'), eviction_policy='evict_last')
tmp44 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + (6864  + x6),   mask=pred6 & xmask, other=float('-inf'), eviction_policy='evict_last')
tmp47 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + (7392  + x6),   mask=pred7 & xmask, other=float('-inf'), eviction_policy='evict_last')
tmp50 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + (7920  + x6),   mask=pred8 & xmask, other=float('-inf'), eviction_policy='evict_last')
applicable_when: Kernel performs stencil or pooling operations with multiple overlapping loads per output element (e.g., 3x3, 5x5 windows); L1/TEX hit rate is very low (<5%); L2 hit rate is high (>70%); CPIStall rule identifies L1TEX dependency stalls as >40% of stall cycles; Eligible Warps Per Scheduler is low (<3.0); the access pattern spans a large byte range per warp but neighboring CTAs share input regions.
do_not_apply_when: Kernel is purely streaming with no spatial reuse between threads or blocks (evict_last wastes L1 capacity); L1 hit rate is already high (>20%); the stencil window is so large it exceeds L1 capacity per SM (e.g., offsets span >50KB), making retention futile; kernel is bandwidth-bound rather than latency-bound (Memory SOL >> Compute SOL).
framework_notes: In Triton, eviction_policy='evict_last' maps to PTX cache operator .L1::evict_last, which pins the cache line in L1 until explicitly evicted. This is a zero-cost semantic hint — no change to instruction count, register count, or grid/block configuration. The equivalent in CUDA C++ is __ldg() or __builtin_nontemporal_load with cache hints. On Hopper/Ampere, this hint is respected by the hardware and can reduce L1TEX stall latency for overlapping stencil access patterns where adjacent CTAs share input data.

strategy_title: Add num_stages=1 to Autotune Configs for Register-Saturated Kernels
strategy_description: Adding num_stages=1 explicitly to all @triton.autotune configs for a register-saturated kernel (32 regs/thread, 64-thread block) achieved a 12.5% speedup (7.87 µs → 7.68 µs) with no change in executed instruction count, block size, grid size, or waves per SM. The improvement is subtle: elapsed cycles dropped from 11416 to 11177 while SM Active Cycles dropped from 6272 to 6065, suggesting the compiler generated a slightly more efficient instruction schedule when software pipelining was explicitly disabled (num_stages=1 vs. default num_stages=3). For non-looping pointwise kernels at register pressure limits, the default num_stages>1 may cause the compiler to over-allocate pipeline state registers or generate suboptimal instruction ordering, and explicitly setting num_stages=1 removes this overhead.
applicable_when: Kernel is at or near register pressure ceiling (registers_per_thread >= 28, Block Limit Registers close to Block Limit Warps); kernel body has no explicit reduction/scan loop (purely pointwise or stencil); default num_stages is not explicitly set in autotune configs (Triton defaults to num_stages=3); CPIStall rule is active with L1TEX dependency stalls; instruction count is already minimized and further reductions are not possible.
do_not_apply_when: Kernel contains explicit tl.range loops where software pipelining (num_stages>1) provides genuine latency hiding for memory loads; kernel is not register-pressure-limited (registers_per_thread < 20 and Block Limit Registers >> Block Limit Warps); the kernel is memory-bandwidth-bound (Memory SOL >> 60%) where pipelining helps overlap compute and memory.
framework_notes: In Triton, num_stages controls the software pipelining depth for loops. For non-looping kernels (no tl.range), the default num_stages=3 may still affect how the compiler schedules instructions and allocates registers for pipeline state. Setting num_stages=1 explicitly disables this pipelining overhead. The equivalent concept in CUDA is the __launch_bounds__ directive or manually unrolling loops with explicit prefetch distances. On Hopper (sm_90), the compiler is particularly sensitive to num_stages for register allocation in kernels near the 32-register-per-thread boundary.

strategy_title: Reducing num_warps to 1 Cuts Instructions but Starves Scheduler
strategy_description: Reducing num_warps from 2 to 1 (block size 64→32) via autotune caused autotune to select the 32-thread block, cutting total executed instructions by 26% (2.0M→1.49M) and Warp Cycles Per Issued Instruction from 15.8 to 9.68, yielding a marginal 1.09x speedup. However, achieved occupancy collapsed from 61.9% to 26.9% and theoretical occupancy dropped to 50% (registers per thread jumped from 32 to 50, limiting blocks/SM). The No-Eligible scheduler stall rate worsened dramatically (35.8%→56.4%) and Eligible Warps Per Scheduler fell from 2.42 to 0.96, indicating severe scheduler starvation — the single warp per block cannot hide L1TEX latency. The speedup is marginal because instruction count reduction is partially offset by increased per-cycle stall overhead from insufficient warp-level parallelism.
applicable_when: Kernel has high ALU/predicate overhead per element (many boolean intermediates), instruction count is the dominant cost, and the kernel is NOT latency-bound by memory (L2 hit rate >70%, memory throughput is not the bottleneck). Waves per SM is already ~2 so occupancy reduction does not increase waves.
do_not_apply_when: Kernel already has low Eligible Warps Per Scheduler (<2.0) or high No-Eligible stall rate (>40%) — reducing to num_warps=1 will worsen scheduler starvation and the single warp cannot hide L1TEX latency. Also avoid when registers per thread increases substantially with smaller block sizes (e.g., 32→50), as this limits theoretical occupancy to 50% and compounds the starvation problem. The diminishing returns are clear: going from num_warps=4→2 gave 1.12x speedup (exp_002), but num_warps=2→1 gave only 1.09x despite a larger absolute instruction reduction.
framework_notes: In Triton, num_warps=1 yields a 32-thread block (1 warp). At this extreme, the compiler may allocate significantly more registers per thread (32→50 observed here) because it has fewer live-value sharing opportunities across warps, which caps theoretical occupancy at 50% on H200 (Block Limit Registers=36 blocks/SM with 50 regs/thread). The net effect is a diminishing-returns regime: each halving of num_warps gives less speedup than the previous because scheduler starvation increasingly offsets instruction count savings. The exp_002 item (num_warps=4→2, 1.12x) should be preferred over this item (num_warps=2→1, 1.09x) as the better operating point.

strategy_title: num_stages Pipelining for Masked Loads Yields Mixed Results
strategy_description: Adding num_stages=2/3 to autotune configs for a 3x3 max-pool kernel caused autotune to select a 32-thread block (num_warps=1, num_stages=1), reducing executed instructions from 2.0M to 1.53M and Warp Cycles Per Issued Instruction from 15.8 to 9.58, but simultaneously collapsing achieved occupancy from 61.9% to 26.7% and increasing No-Eligible stalls from 35.8% to 54.5%. The net result was a marginal 7.6% speedup despite elapsed cycles actually increasing (11416 → 11780). The speedup appears to be driven by the autotune selecting a smaller block size (32 vs 64 threads) rather than by software pipelining itself — the selected config was num_stages=1, not 2 or 3. Adding num_stages variants to autotune configs for pointwise kernels with complex masked loads does not guarantee that the compiler generates async prefetch instructions; the autotune may simply select a lower num_warps config that reduces instruction count at the cost of occupancy.
fast_pseudocode:
@triton.autotune(
    configs=[
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=1, num_stages=1),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=1, num_stages=2),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=1, num_stages=3),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=2, num_stages=1),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=2, num_stages=2),
    ],
    key=['xnumel'],
)
@triton.jit
def kernel(in_ptr0, out_ptr0, xnumel, XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    # 9 masked loads with evict_last
    tmp11 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + offset, mask=pred & xmask, other=-inf, eviction_policy='evict_last')
    ...
    tl.store(out_ptr0 + x6, result, mask=xmask, eviction_policy='evict_first')
# autotune selects num_warps=1, num_stages=1 -> block_size=32, registers=48, achieved_occupancy=26.7%
applicable_when: Kernel has high L1TEX CPIStall (>40% of CPI) and the autotune search space does not include low num_warps configs (num_warps=1). Adding num_stages variants alongside num_warps=1 may allow autotune to discover a smaller block size that reduces total instruction count even if software pipelining itself is not activated.
do_not_apply_when: Kernel already has num_warps=1 in its autotune search space; the dominant bottleneck is occupancy (achieved occupancy already below 30%); the kernel uses complex masked loads with compound boolean predicates where Triton's compiler is unlikely to generate async prefetch instructions for num_stages>1. Do not expect num_stages>1 to activate software pipelining for pointwise kernels with 9+ masked conditional loads — the compiler typically only pipelines simple, unconditional loads.
framework_notes: In Triton, num_stages controls software pipelining depth for tl.load instructions. For matmul kernels with tl.dot, num_stages=2/3 reliably generates async copy prefetch instructions. For pointwise kernels with complex masked loads (compound boolean predicates), the compiler may not generate async prefetch even with num_stages>1. In this experiment, the winning autotune config was num_stages=1 (no pipelining), suggesting the benefit came from the smaller block size (32 threads) reducing instruction count rather than from pipelining. The equivalent CUDA concept is __pipeline_memcpy_async, which also requires simple, unconditional loads to be effective.

strategy_title: Cap Registers via maxnreg to Increase SM Block Concurrency
strategy_description: Adding maxnreg=24 to triton.Config reduced registers per thread from 32 to 24, which increased Block Limit Registers from 32 to 42 blocks/SM, allowing more concurrent blocks. Despite achieved occupancy slightly decreasing (61.9% → 59.4%), scheduler No-Eligible stalls dropped (35.8% → 31.0%) and Eligible Warps Per Scheduler improved (2.42 → 3.08), yielding a 6.3% speedup. The instruction count increased by ~25% (2.0M → 2.5M), indicating the compiler spilled some register values to L1 scratch, but the H200's large L1 and high L2 hit rate (80%) made spill loads cheap enough that the net effect was positive. The speedup is modest because the kernel remains latency-bound (CPIStall L1TEX dependency still ~46% of stall cycles) and the occupancy improvement was smaller than predicted.
applicable_when: Kernel has high registers per thread (≥28) relative to block size, causing Block Limit Registers to be the binding occupancy constraint; achieved occupancy is significantly below theoretical (gap >30pp); CPIStall 'not-selected' stalls are moderate (>20% of CPI); L2 hit rate is high (>70%) making register spill loads to L1/L2 cheap; the kernel body has complex predicate chains or many live values that drive register pressure.
do_not_apply_when: Block Limit Registers is already not the binding constraint (i.e., Block Limit Warps or Block Limit Shared Mem is lower); the kernel is already bandwidth-bound (Memory SOL > 70%); register spill traffic would exceed L1 capacity and cause L2 pressure; the kernel has very few registers per thread (<20) where capping would have no effect; when the instruction count increase from spills (observed ~25% here) would outweigh the occupancy benefit.
framework_notes: In Triton, maxnreg is passed as a kwarg to triton.Config() (e.g., triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=2, maxnreg=24)). This is a compiler directive that caps the register file allocation per thread, potentially forcing the compiler to spill values to L1 scratch space. The equivalent in CUDA C++ is __launch_bounds__(max_threads_per_block, min_blocks_per_sm) or the maxrregcount ptxas flag. On H200 with 65536 registers/SM: at 32 regs × 64 threads/block = 2048 regs/block → 32 blocks/SM; at 24 regs × 64 threads/block = 1536 regs/block → 42 blocks/SM. The speedup was positive but modest (6.3%) because achieved occupancy did not improve as predicted — the binding constraint shifted to other factors (warp scheduling overhead, L1TEX latency stalls).
